benefits: Lists exactly who may send mail as your domain — the foundation DMARC builds on.
Counts DNS lookups live, so you never ship a record that breaks the 10-lookup limit.
Validates every IP and hostname as you type — typos are caught before they reach DNS.
Warns against dangerous choices like +all before you publish them.
Runs entirely in your browser; your mail setup is never uploaded.

faqs.a: As a TXT record on your bare domain (example.com), not a subdomain. Add it in your DNS provider's panel. There must be only one SPF record per domain — two records invalidate each other.
faqs.q: Where do I publish the SPF record?

faqs.a: Receivers stop evaluating after 10 DNS-querying mechanisms (include, a, mx, ptr, exists, redirect) and return permerror — which usually fails closed. ip4/ip6 don't count. This tool counts them for you; nested includes inside a provider's record also count, so leave headroom.
faqs.q: What is the 10 DNS lookup limit?

faqs.a: -all (fail) tells receivers to reject non-matching mail — the strict, recommended ending once everything works. ~all (softfail) marks it suspicious but usually still delivers — the safe choice while testing. ?all is neutral (no policy) and +all passes everything, which defeats the purpose.

No — that's exactly what include: is for. Your marketing platform publishes its own SPF record (like _spf.google.com); you include it and they maintain their IPs. Never copy someone's IP list into ip4: entries — it goes stale.
faqs.q: Should I list my provider's IPs directly?

faqs.a: redirect= replaces your entire record with another domain's SPF record — useful when a provider manages SPF for you. When redirect is set, no other mechanisms are allowed in the record. Most setups don't need it; include: covers the common cases.

They're unrelated mechanisms that happen to share a name: SPF (Sender Policy Framework) authorizes sending IPs for email, while sunscreen SPF measures UV protection. Your mail server does not need sunscreen.
faqs.q: Is email SPF related to sunscreen SPF?

spf-record-generator.formula:
v=spf1 [mx] [a] [ip4:addr ...] [ip6:addr ...] [include:host ...] { -all | ~all | ?all | +all }
or: v=spf1 redirect=other.example

Lookup budget (max 10): mx=1, a=1, each include:=1, redirect=1. ip4:/ip6: cost nothing.
Record should fit in 255 characters (one DNS string).
howTo: Enter your domain and tick mx if your own mail server sends directly.
Add your sending IPs (ip4/ip6), one per line — CIDR ranges like 203.0.113.0/24 work too.
Add one include: per email provider (Google, Microsoft 365, your marketing platform).
Choose the all qualifier: ~all while testing, -all when everything works.
Watch the lookup counter stay at or under 10, then copy the record and publish it as a TXT record on your domain.
keyFacts: SPF (Sender Policy Framework) is a DNS TXT record listing which IPs may send mail for your domain.
Receivers check the envelope sender's IP against your record; mismatches fail SPF.
Mechanisms: mx (your mail servers), a (your web server), ip4:/ip6: (explicit addresses), include: (a provider's record).
The record ends with an all mechanism: -all (fail), ~all (softfail), ?all (neutral), +all (pass).
SPF has a hard 10 DNS lookup limit — exceeding it causes permerror and failed checks.
SPF alone only checks the envelope domain; DMARC adds alignment with the visible From header.
spf-record-generator.keywords: spf record generator, spf txt record, spf dns record, sender policy framework generator

labels.dnsNote: Publish this as a TXT record on your bare domain (not a subdomain). DNS changes usually take effect within a few hours.
labels.includesHint: One hostname per line, e.g. _spf.google.com. Each include costs one DNS lookup.
labels.redirectHint: Replaces the whole record with another domain's SPF. Leave empty for normal setups.
labels.useA: a — authorize the domain's A record
labels.useAHint: Authorizes the IP your domain resolves to (your web server).
labels.useMxHint: Authorizes the IPs of your domain's MX records.
labels.warnInvalidHost: Some include/redirect hostnames are invalid and were left out.
labels.warnInvalidIp: Some IP addresses are invalid and were left out of the record.
labels.warnPlusAll: +all passes every sender in the world — it defeats the purpose of SPF. Use -all or ~all.
labels.warnRecordTooLong: The record exceeds 255 characters and may need splitting across multiple DNS strings.
labels.warnTooManyLookups: Over the 10 DNS lookup limit — receivers will return permerror. Remove includes or replace them with ip4 entries.

limitations: Only authorizes IPs — it says nothing about message content or legitimacy.
Checks the envelope domain, not the visible From address; DMARC alignment closes that gap.
Forwarding can break SPF (the forwarder's IP isn't listed) — SRS or DKIM-based DMARC handles that.
Nested includes inside a provider's record also consume your 10-lookup budget — leave headroom.

spf-record-generator.quickAnswer: An SPF record is a DNS TXT record on your domain listing which servers may send mail as you. For example, v=spf1 mx ip4:203.0.113.10 include:_spf.google.com ~all authorizes your mail servers, one IP, and Google's servers, while ~all softly fails everything else. Receivers allow only 10 DNS lookups per check — this generator counts them live so your record never breaks the limit.

Domain example.com: mx ticked, ip4 203.0.113.10, include _spf.google.com, qualifier ~all.

v=spf1 mx ip4:203.0.113.10 include:_spf.google.com ~all
Checks traced by the tool:
1. Mechanisms: mx + ip4:203.0.113.10 (valid IPv4) + include:_spf.google.com (valid hostname).
2. DNS lookups: mx (1) + include (1) = 2 of 10 — safely under the limit. ip4: costs nothing.
3. Length: 55 characters — well under the 255-character single-string limit.
4. Qualifier ~all: safe while testing; switch to -all once mail flows correctly.
